meta.title: SAS-to-Python/R Conversion Rulebook
meta.purpose: Machine-consumable guardrail knowledge base for AI-assisted translation pipelines.
meta.source_ids_note: Source IDs [S-nn] resolve to the annotated source inventory.

contract: One blessed target per language per rule. Alternates are allowed only when the rule's alternates_when condition is met.
required_settings are mandatory, not advisory. Omitting one is a defect.
forbidden_patterns must never appear in generated code.
equivalence_class NO-DIRECT-EQUIVALENT => STOP. Emit a human-review ticket, never generated code.
Every translated unit ships with its validation_test wired into the golden-master harness against stored SAS reference output.

global_policies.name: language-routing
global_policies.rule: Complex survey estimation (SURVEYMEANS/FREQ/REG/LOGISTIC/PHREG/SELECT, replicate weights, calibration) and mixed models with repeated-measures covariance structures (MIXED/GLIMMIX) MUST target R. Python is forbidden as primary target for these families. statsmodels MixedLM and archived samplics are not acceptable substitutes. [S-36, S-39, CAMIS]

global_policies.name: no-dynamic-code
global_policies.rule: Never emit eval(), exec(), or eval(parse(text=)). CALL EXECUTE, %sysfunc code generation, and macro code-fragment substitution route to human review.

global_policies.name: data-conversion-first
global_policies.rule: sas7bdat is read exactly once, at migration time, with pyreadstat (user_missing=True) or haven (catalog_file= when a format catalog exists). Output: Parquet (zstd) plus a metadata sidecar (variable labels, format names, special-missing tags). Downstream code reads Parquet only. Validate the conversion against SAS row counts and per-column checksums before use.

global_policies.name: dependency-pinning
global_policies.rule: Every project carries a lockfile (renv.lock pinned to a dated Posit Package Manager snapshot; uv.lock or conda-lock on conda-forge). No unpinned installs. Avoid the Anaconda defaults channel. Version floors from meta section.

global_policies.name: package-allowlist
global_policies.rule: Only allowlisted packages may appear in generated code. RED-rated packages (samplics) are forbidden. YELLOW-rated packages (statsmodels, lifelines, pyreadstat, pandera, survey, srvyr, forecast) are allowed with pinned versions and quarterly health review.

global_policies.name: validation-mandatory
global_policies.rule: Every translated program unit ships with a golden-master test comparing its output to stored SAS reference output at the rule's tolerance tier, run on the standard trap fixture (duplicate BY keys both sides, missing values including special missings, -2.5, month-end dates, mixed-case blank-padded strings).

global_policies.name: settings-before-numbers
global_policies.rule: When a comparison fails, first audit required_settings. Documented default differences explain nearly all SAS vs open-source discrepancies (CAMIS finding). Only escalate a numerical difference after settings are proven pinned.

global_policies.name: upgrade-cadence
global_policies.rule: On any major release of a blessed package, re-run the full trap-fixture regression suite before adopting. Quarterly: review CAMIS updates, YELLOW package maintainer status (survey package succession above all), and this rulebook's version floors.

global_policies.name: iml-routing
global_policies.rule: PROC IML (and any SAS/IML matrix-language program) routes to human review before code generation, except for the matrix surface pinned and gated in MX-001 (concatenation, transpose, multiplication, the 2x2 inverse). Everything else in IML (general inversions, subscript conventions, missing handling in matrix operations, module syntax) stays review-gated until its own scope is pinned.

rules.sas_pattern: SET a b; (concatenation)

python_target.pattern: pd.concat([a, b], ignore_index=True)

r_target.pattern: bind_rows(a, b)

rules.alternates_when: large data: polars pl.concat(how='diagonal'); duckdb UNION ALL BY NAME
required_settings: ignore_index=True
post-concat dtype audit
forbidden_patterns: append in a loop
rbind in a loop
silent_difference_checks: SAS truncates differing char lengths silently; verify max string widths
rules.validation_test: row count == sum of inputs; column set == union; dtypes vs PROC CONTENTS
rules.confidence: high

rules.sas_pattern: MERGE a b; BY key; (1:1 or 1:many)

python_target.pattern: a.merge(b, on='key', how='outer', validate='one_to_many', indicator=True)

r_target.pattern: full_join(a, b, by='key', relationship='one-to-many')

required_settings: how='outer' for default MERGE
validate=/relationship= mandatory
replicate IN= logic with indicator/anti_join
re-sort output before comparison
forbidden_patterns: merge without validate/relationship
silent suffix collisions on overlapping non-BY variables
silent_difference_checks: overlapping non-BY variables: SAS overwrites from rightmost dataset; joins create _x/_y; resolve explicitly
rules.validation_test: sorted full outer join row-for-row vs SAS output
rules.confidence: high

rules.sas_pattern: MERGE with BY where BOTH datasets repeat BY values (many-to-many)
rules.rationale: SAS pairs rows positionally within the BY group, retaining the last row of the shorter side (max(n,m) rows). Every join produces n*m rows. No join reproduces SAS. Faithful port needs per-group row counters + outer join on (key, seq) + group-wise ffill of the shorter side, but usually the SAS behavior is a latent bug requiring sign-off on SQL semantics instead.
rules.detection: per-key group-size cross-tab of both inputs; flag any key with n>1 AND m>1; also grep legacy logs for 'more than one data set with repeats of BY values'
rules.confidence: high

rules.sas_pattern: UPDATE master txns; BY key;

python_target.pattern: master.set_index(k).update(collapse_last_nonmissing(txns)); # .update skips NaN, matching UPDATE

r_target.pattern: rows_update(master, txns |> group_by(key) |> summarize(across(everything(), ~last(na.omit(.x)))), by='key')

required_settings: collapse transactions to last non-missing per variable per key first
new keys in transactions: rows_upsert
silent_difference_checks: special missing ._ in a transaction SETS the master value to missing in SAS; requires sentinel encoding
UPDATEMODE=NOMISSINGCHECK changes the rule
rules.validation_test: per-variable per-key equality on fixture with multi-transaction keys and deliberate missings
rules.confidence: medium

rules.sas_pattern: IF-THEN/ELSE ladder deriving a variable

python_target.pattern: np.select([conds...], [values...], default=)

r_target.pattern: case_when(c1 ~ v1, ..., .default = v)

required_settings: EXPLICIT missing arm FIRST for every inequality on a nullable variable
forbidden_patterns: bare x < N condition on a nullable column without an is-missing guard
silent_difference_checks: SAS: . < 0 is TRUE; missings land in the low bucket. Python/R: row falls to ELSE. Bare 'if x' in SAS is false for 0 AND missing
rules.validation_test: derived-variable frequency table incl. a missing-input stratum vs PROC FREQ
rules.confidence: high

rules.sas_pattern: FIRST.var / LAST.var / RETAIN / sum statement / counters

python_target.pattern: stable sort; g=df.groupby(keys, dropna=False); first=~df.duplicated(keys); last=~df.duplicated(keys, keep='last'); run=df.assign(_x=df[c].fillna(0)).groupby(keys, dropna=False)['_x'].cumsum(); ctr=g.cumcount()+1

r_target.pattern: arrange(...) |> group_by(...) |> mutate(first=row_number()==1, last=row_number()==n(), run=cumsum(coalesce(x,0)), ctr=row_number())

required_settings: stable sort with SAS-identical order incl. missing-first
fillna(0)/coalesce before cumsum (sum statement treats missing increment as 0)
pandas groupby dropna=False (SAS keeps the missing BY group)
fill the column BEFORE grouping: SeriesGroupBy.fillna was removed in pandas 3, so the cumulative sum has to come from a pre-filled column instead of an aggregation call
the pattern is executed over multiple groups in saschi/test_rulebook.py rather than trusted
silent_difference_checks: ungrouped RETAIN carries across BY boundaries; match scoping
WHERE applied before FIRST./LAST. changes flags; subsetting IF after does not
rules.validation_test: (key, first, last, running_sum) tuples row-for-row after identical sort
rules.confidence: high

rules.sas_pattern: LAG/DIF invocation queues, including bounded direct assignment in conditional actions

python_target.pattern: two cases preserve different invocation schedules. An unconditional CALL SITE with conditional use of its result advances on every row. A call INSIDE conditional logic advances only when that branch runs, so a row shift is wrong. The runtime uses per-DATA-step numeric occurrence queues keyed by structural source-operation path, advancing only on direct RHS execution. Existing raw reference fixtures remain separate evidence.

r_target.pattern: Original raw queue fixtures plus lag_execution.R prior-invoked-index execution model; no row-shift replacement of conditional calls.

required_settings: Canonical LAG/DIF and LAG1..LAG100/DIF1..DIF100, one argument, direct assignment RHS only. Selected IF/ELSE and counted-DO leaves are admitted under their existing contracts. Preserve source behavior without guessing or repairing the author intent. Other conditional/stateful contexts remain review cases.

Preserve whether the CALL SITE itself is conditional, rather than only its result use. Each source occurrence owns its own queue, initially missing. Structural path keys distinguish identical or aliased operations; row/loop iteration is not part of the key. State lasts for one DATA step and resets for each new step/run. BY boundaries and repeated OUTPUT do not reset/advance queues.

Argument is a finite numeric or ordinary-missing literal, numeric variable or _N_. Ordinary missing is enqueued. Character, tagged-missing and nonfinite values, other reserved automatic references and argument expressions remain refused.

Validate literal/type/descriptor policy even on empty/filtered input and skipped branches/bodies. Dynamic invalid values and nonfinite DIF results refuse atomically; helper queue state is not changed by an invalid call. No SAS error-state/diagnostic equivalence claimed.

Nested calls, arithmetic/function consumers, predicates/WHERE, arrays, PUT_ALL and C++ queue execution are deferred. A conditional use of an unconditional result differs from conditional invocation; do not transform between them.
forbidden_patterns: translating a conditional LAG call as a column shift (returns the previous ROW where SAS returns the previous EXECUTION)
silent_difference_checks: SAS LAG is a queue: executed conditionally it returns the value at the previous EXECUTION, not the previous row. Direct translation of conditional LAG is wrong
each LAG occurrence carries its own queue, so two calls in one statement have independent history
a BY-group boundary does not itself execute or reset a queue
LAGn and DIFn carry a queue of depth n, so the first n executions return missing
a missing argument is still an execution: it returns the front and stores missing, which is why a skipped call and a call with a missing argument leave different histories
DIF differences against the same occurrence's queue, so it inherits the invocation history rather than the row order
rules.validation_test: values 10,20,30,40 with the occurrence executed only on rows two and four: SAS returns missing then 20, where a full-column shift returns 10 and 30. Executed two ways: the pattern's counterpart in saschi/test_rulebook.py, and the byte-equal Python/R gate examples/verify_lag.py, which also pins LAGn depth, the independent occurrence queues, DIF, and the missing-argument push Preserve examples/verify_lag.py unchanged. examples/verify_lag_execution.py, original examples/lag_execution.R and saschi.test_lag_execution add complete source-runtime prior-invocation comparisons, distinct occurrence identities, branch/loop scheduling, filter/BY/output timing, reset boundaries and atomic/local refusals.
rules.confidence: bounded repository/base-R evidence; no live SAS

rules.sas_pattern: PROC SORT (incl. NODUPKEY)

python_target.pattern: df.sort_values(by, kind='stable', na_position='first'); NODUPKEY: + .drop_duplicates(subset=keys, keep='first')

r_target.pattern: arrange(across(keys, ~ .x), .locale='C') with NA-first pre-sort: arrange(!is.na(x), x); NODUPKEY: distinct(across(keys), .keep_all=TRUE); or data.table setkey (NA-first native)

required_settings: kind='stable' (pandas default is NOT stable)
na_position='first' (pandas default last)
NA-first handling in R (dplyr default last)
pin collation to C/byte order for mixed-case keys
SQL: NULLS FIRST
silent_difference_checks: NA position flips which row NODUPKEY keeps and flips FIRST. flags
special missings ._ < . < .A-.Z sort order collapses to NA; recode to companion column BEFORE sorting if meaningful
rules.validation_test: checksum of key sequence after sort incl. NA and mixed-case rows; NODUPKEY survivor row IDs identical
rules.confidence: high

rules.sas_pattern: PROC TRANSPOSE

python_target.pattern: pivot_table(index=ids, columns=name, values=val, aggfunc='last') where the SAS step specified LET / melt(id_vars=ids). Without LET a duplicate ID is an error in SAS, so the port raises instead of choosing a row.

r_target.pattern: pivot_wider(names_from, values_from, values_fn=last) only where LET was specified / pivot_longer(cols)

required_settings: aggfunc='last' / values_fn=last ONLY where the SAS step specified LET. LET is what makes last-observation behaviour the documented contract rather than a lucky choice
without LET, preserve the failure: a duplicate ID must raise, not silently keep one
forbidden_patterns: pivot_table default aggfunc (silently averages duplicates)
aggfunc='last' applied to a step that did not specify LET (converts a SAS error into a silent pick)
silent_difference_checks: mixed numeric+char transposes: SAS converts all to char
no-ID transpose generates COL1..COLn: replicate with within-group cumcount
duplicate formatted IDs stop processing without LET, and keep the last occurrence with it
rules.validation_test: identical wide shape; a duplicate ID with LET keeps the last occurrence and the same input without LET raises. Executed in saschi/test_rulebook.py
rules.confidence: high

rules.sas_pattern: PROC FORMAT used as recode or display labels

python_target.pattern: value maps: s.map(fmt_dict).fillna(other_default); ranges: pd.cut(x, bins, labels, right=False) for low-<high; keep raw value + label as TWO columns

r_target.pattern: case_when / factor(levels, labels); ranges: cut(right=FALSE); haven labelled -> as_factor()

required_settings: export legacy catalogs via PROC FORMAT CNTLOUT= and implement as a versioned join table
interval closure matched to SAS range syntax
OTHER= mapped to explicit default
forbidden_patterns: recoding the analysis variable in place (destroys stored value)
silent_difference_checks: SAS PROCs group by FORMATTED value; a port grouping by raw values gets different groups
MULTILABEL formats are a many-to-many join; flag for review
rules.validation_test: PROC FREQ of formatted variable vs value_counts of label column
rules.confidence: high

rules.sas_pattern: SAS dates/datetimes/times (epoch 1960-01-01)

python_target.pattern: ingest via pyreadstat (auto-converts); manual: to_datetime(x, unit='D'|'s', origin='1960-01-01'); INTNX/INTCK: period arithmetic .dt.to_period()

r_target.pattern: auto-converts; manual: as.Date(x, origin='1960-01-01'), as.POSIXct(..., tz='UTC'); intervals via lubridate periods on floor_date boundaries

required_settings: date-vs-datetime decided from FORMAT metadata, never magnitude
tz-naive handling explicit
INTCK counts boundary crossings: use period subtraction, not relativedelta
silent_difference_checks: misclassified datetime-as-date is off by factor 86400
two-digit years: verify against YEARCUTOFF window
pre-1677 dates overflow datetime64[ns]: use datetime64[us]/pyarrow timestamps
rules.validation_test: min/max/mean of converted column vs SAS; round-trip 01JAN1960=0
rules.confidence: high

rules.sas_pattern: ROUND(x, unit)

python_target.pattern: np.sign(x)*np.floor(np.abs(x)/u + 0.5)*u  # half away from zero

r_target.pattern: round_half_up(x, digits)

forbidden_patterns: builtin round() in Python or R for SAS-parity code (banker's rounding: 2.5 -> 2; SAS: 2.5 -> 3)
silent_difference_checks: rare 1-ulp float boundary cases remain (SAS fuzzes); verify on real data
rules.confidence: high

rules.sas_pattern: MOD(a,b), bounded exact integers; INT(x) remains unwired

python_target.pattern: sas_semantics.sas_mod(a,b)

r_target.pattern: sas_mod(a,b) from examples/mod.R; exact binary long division

required_settings: Exactly two numeric operands, each finite and integer-valued with magnitude <= 2**53, the binary64 exact-integer limit; the divisor must be nonzero.
The supported domain applies to evaluated binary64 operands after the existing literal/catalog normalization. The Python reference also rejects oversized Python integers before conversion.
Nonzero results follow the dividend sign, regardless of divisor sign; exact divisions return zero.
Missing and tagged missing, nonnumeric, nonfinite, fractional, oversized, and zero-divisor inputs require review. These are implementation refusals, not a claim that SAS refuses each of those inputs.
SAS floating-point fuzzing near zero or the divisor and insufficient-precision missing/log behavior are not implemented. INT and MODZ remain unwired; C++ refuses MOD calls.
forbidden_patterns: raw signed-operand Python % or R %% for SAS MOD parity (divisor sign: -7%3=2, SAS=-1); the reference instead takes magnitude remainder then applies the dividend sign
unbounded fmod or a-b*trunc(a/b) as complete SAS MOD parity (fuzzing and quotient cancellation differ)
claiming INT parity from this MOD gate
silent_difference_checks: SAS documents exactness within the host exact-integer range and fuzzes general floating remainders. This gate bounds both operand magnitudes by 2**53 and does not substitute fmod for fractional MOD.
Repository pins, constructive arithmetic cases, Python fmod on the integer domain, and independent base-R binary long division are implementation evidence; no live SAS output is claimed.
rules.validation_test: examples/verify_mod.py: dividend/divisor sign combinations, zero, exact division, 2**53 boundaries, constructive cases and refusal boundaries; saschi.test_functions.ModFunctionTests: routing, emitted runtime, typed catalogs, expressions, arity and C++ refusal
rules.confidence: high

rules.sas_pattern: SUM(a,b,...) function

python_target.pattern: df[cols].sum(axis=1)  # skipna

r_target.pattern: rowSums(cbind(a,b), na.rm=TRUE)

forbidden_patterns: a + b as a port of SUM() (propagates missing; SUM() skips it)
rules.validation_test: rows with partial missing match SAS SUM output
rules.confidence: high

rules.sas_pattern: Character functions (SCAN, CATX, SUBSTR, INDEX, TRANWRD, COMPRESS, PUT/INPUT)

python_target.pattern: vectorized .str methods with 1-based offsets corrected; CATX: delimiter-join skipping NA; INPUT: to_numeric(errors='coerce') + coercion count logged

r_target.pattern: word()/str_sub()/str_locate()/str_replace_all(fixed())/str_remove_all(); CATX: tidyr::unite(na.rm=TRUE); INPUT: readr::parse_number()

required_settings: SCAN collapses consecutive delimiters: regex split, not literal split
regex=False / fixed() for literal replacement
strip trailing blanks on ingest (SAS fixed-width comparison semantics)
INDEX absent: SAS 0 vs find -1
rules.validation_test: fixture with empty strings, doubled blanks, missing, multibyte chars
rules.confidence: high

rules.sas_pattern: ARRAY + DO loop over variables

python_target.pattern: vectorized: df[cols] = df[cols].replace(...); loop-carried logic: melt -> operate -> pivot back

r_target.pattern: across(all_of(cols), fn); loop-carried: pivot_longer -> mutate -> pivot_wider

required_settings: OUTPUT inside a DO loop = row multiplication: port as explode/uncount, never mutate
silent_difference_checks: x1--y (double-dash) name ranges depend on PDV column order; resolve the actual list from PROC CONTENTS
rules.validation_test: aggregate over recoded columns; row-count multiplier for OUTPUT loops
rules.confidence: high

rules.sas_pattern: Hash object lookup in DATA step

python_target.pattern: merge(how='left', validate='many_to_one') or Series.map(dict)

r_target.pattern: left_join(relationship='many-to-one'); scale: keyed data.table update join

required_settings: many_to_one validation mandatory: SAS hash find() kept the FIRST duplicate silently; unvalidated join fans out rows
rules.validation_test: output row count == input row count
rules.confidence: high

rules.sas_pattern: Reading sas7bdat/xpt; LIBNAME libraries

python_target.pattern: read_sas7bdat(path, user_missing=True) once -> Parquet + metadata sidecar (GP-03)

r_target.pattern: read_sas(path, catalog_file=) once -> Parquet + sidecar

forbidden_patterns: pd.read_sas in production pipelines (no metadata, no user_missing, encoding bugs)
repeated sas7bdat parsing downstream
silent_difference_checks: encoding= for WLATIN1 sessions
unformatted date-valued numerics arrive as raw day/second counts
rules.validation_test: n rows/cols, per-column sum/mean/nmiss, PROC FREQ of key categoricals, hash of sorted key
rules.confidence: high

rules.sas_pattern: Special missing values .A-.Z, ._
rules.rule: At Parquet conversion, materialize special missings into an explicit companion category column (e.g. x_missreason in {A,B,D,R,...}). haven tagged_na is lost silently by many operations; do not rely on it downstream.
rules.validation_test: cross-tab of x_missreason vs SAS special-missing frequencies
rules.confidence: high

rules.sas_pattern: Significant-digit rounding and rendering (four sig figs)

python_target.pattern: unit = 10**(floor(log10(abs(x))) - n + 1); round half-away at unit; then PUT-style fixed format. NEVER '%g' alone

r_target.pattern: unit = 10^(floor(log10(abs(x))) - n + 1); half-away at unit; then formatC. NEVER sprintf('%g') or signif() alone

required_settings: SAS has no %g format: sig figs come from ROUND to an explicit power-of-ten unit, then a normal format
R sprintf('%g'), Python '%g', and R signif() all round half to even; SAS ROUND is half away from zero, so 0.125@2 is 0.13 in SAS and 0.12 in both open languages
SAS ROUND fuzz absorbs representation error: 9.995@3 is 10.0 in SAS, 9.99 in %g
the 2**53 cliff applies to the unit exponent: compute the unit in float, never by string truncation
silent_difference_checks: %g switches to scientific notation by magnitude (threshold 1e-4 and 1e5 by default), while the SAS pattern renders fixed: pin the render style separately from the rounding
rules.confidence: high

rules.sas_pattern: PROC IMPORT dbms=csv type inference (guessingrows window)

python_target.pattern: explicit dtype per column; identifiers as dtype=str; never trust default inference for identifiers or windowed columns

r_target.pattern: read.csv(colClasses=...) explicit; identifiers colClasses='character'; never default inference

required_settings: PROC IMPORT guesses from the first guessingrows non-blank values (default 20): a column clean in the window but dirty later is read NUMERIC by SAS and the late non-numeric becomes missing with a note; pandas and R infer from the whole file and read it character: pin the divergence per file
leading-zero identifiers (zip, ids) are stripped by ALL three defaults: read identifiers as character explicitly
a column of blanks in the window reads CHAR in SAS; pandas/R land float64: normalize empty-but-numeric columns to NUM with missing, not INT
NA tokens differ: pandas default na_values includes 'N/A' and 'null'; R default na.strings is 'NA' only. The same CSV reads missing in pandas and string in R: pin na_values/na.strings per file
silent_difference_checks: the window-vs-full-file mismatch silently changes WHICH values are missing
SAS numeric-looking cells with commas read character in CSV import; pandas/R also: quote the column explicitly
rules.validation_test: fixture: 20 clean rows then a non-numeric token -> SAS NUM (window) vs pandas/R CHAR (full file); leading-zero column byte-preserved under explicit reads
rules.confidence: high

rules.sas_pattern: COUNT(string, substring <, modifiers>)

python_target.pattern: sas_semantics.sas_count(string, substring, modifiers): bounded ASCII literal matching with explicit I/T and overlap refusal

r_target.pattern: examples/count.R sas_count: enumerate literal substring windows, reject overlapping positions, count the remaining matches

required_settings: Case-sensitive by default; I ignores ASCII case; T removes trailing ASCII blanks from both operands; modifier letters accept either case
Preserve leading and trailing blanks unless T applies; do not apply DS-015 ingest trimming to COUNT operands
SAS documents overlapping matches as undefined: detect them after I/T processing and refuse execution for human review
Bounded support policy: refuse zero-length input strings, empty substrings including after T, non-ASCII/NUL text, numeric or null arguments, and modifier characters other than I/T
Blank character variables retain their declared padding; they are not numeric missing values. Python translation and the R reference are gated; the C++ scalar pilot does not support COUNT
forbidden_patterns: Bare Python str.count or R regex counting without the modifier and overlap guards
A numeric expectation for an overlapping match or Python's empty-needle len(string)+1 default
Treating this fixture evidence as a live-SAS comparison or as support for SQL COUNT, COUNTC, or COUNTW
rules.validation_test: examples/verify_count.py: synthetic documented pins, I/T and blank discriminators, refusal pins, exhaustive short-string regex/Python/R agreement; saschi.test_functions checks translated execution and runtime refusal
rules.confidence: high within the bounded slice; repository evidence, no live SAS

rules.sas_pattern: PUT quoted-literal <quoted-literal ...>;

python_target.pattern: sas_semantics.sas_put_literals: concatenate decoded quoted tokens into one logical log record

r_target.pattern: examples/put.R: scan each quoted token and join decoded characters without separators

required_settings: Quoted literals advance to the immediately following column, without an automatic blank. Preserve spaces inside literals; syntax whitespace does not print
Decode doubled delimiters once. In the PUT-specific quote-pair form, two delimiters alone output one delimiter, as documented by PUT Statement: List
Without FILE or a line-hold specifier, each PUT writes a separate log record. This contract stores logical records without newline characters, source echoes, or SAS diagnostic framing
Bounded support policy: only printable ASCII and a total record width at most 64, the minimum documented LINESIZE. Longer records require a wrapping contract

Double-quoted & and % require macro review; single-quoted text remains literal. No implicit conversions, repeats, formatted items, FILE destinations, pointers, line holds, or conditional PUT in this slice. DS-024 separately gates mixed literals and ordinary character variables
Python translation and a base-R reference are gated. The C++ scalar pilot refuses this operation. Existing named-list PUT remains a separate operation
forbidden_patterns: print(*values) or paste(values) with a default blank separator
Trimming literal blanks, applying Python backslash escapes, or treating doubled SAS quotes as two output characters
Dropping an unsupported PUT suffix, expanding macros implicitly, or presenting logical records as a captured physical SAS log
rules.validation_test: examples/verify_put.py: original spacing/quoting pins, generated literal round trips, independent R witness, boundary refusals, and naive-error detectors; saschi.test_put: emitted output, iteration order, source lines, whole-job refusals, target refusal, and unchanged Roku Hello World
rules.confidence: high within the bounded slice; repository evidence, no live SAS

rules.sas_pattern: PUT character-variable <character-variable | quoted-literal ...>; with literals also permitted before the first variable

python_target.pattern: sas_semantics.sas_put_character_list: preserve decoded literal text, trim character-variable edge blanks and advance one blank after each value

r_target.pattern: examples/put_list.R: scan quoted tokens independently and find the first/last occupied character positions

required_settings: Unformatted character variables lose leading and trailing ASCII blanks and receive one following blank; embedded blanks remain. Quoted literals keep their own spaces and add no separator, using DS-023 decoding
The returned logical record includes the final variable separator. This models documented output pointer spacing, not physical SAS log framing or trailing-blank retention by a log destination

Bounded support policy: printable ASCII, at most 64 columns including literal text and every variable separator. Blank and zero-length character values require a separate missing-field contract and are refused; this refusal is not a claim about SAS missing-value behavior

At least one ordinary character variable is required. Reject numeric, uninitialized, tagged-missing, automatic, special PUT control, and formatted variables. Validate descriptor formats even with zero rows, WHERE filtering, or a preceding LENGTH; a newly assigned character copy does not inherit a format

Require original source whitespace immediately after a closing literal delimiter before a variable. Adjacent suffixes and comment-only separation are deferred, even if comment-separated source would be valid SAS. Optional parser spans preserve this distinction without changing normalized text or equality

No numeric/BEST formatting, variable lists, _ALL_, FILE, repeats, pointers, line holds, conditional PUT, macro expansion, or implicit conversions. A program using DS-024 conservatively refuses any original double-quoted source token containing & or %, including unused, future, conditional, and prior-step expressions. Single-quoted source and external catalog values remain data
Python execution and independent base-R logical records are gated; C++ refuses the operation. Named-list output and DS-023 pure literals remain separate operations
forbidden_patterns: Using rstrip alone, inserting a blank before each literal, omitting the variable separator, or trimming the finished logical record
Dropping attached formats or interpreting a typed constant as a literal followed by a variable after whitespace normalization
